statement_tested: VF-25 (reworded, BRIEF_R22.md): Loading the system reveals MCI where the unloaded or static counterpart does not. Within the same study, a measure taken under a more demanding condition (for example dual-task or curved-path walking, peripheral-attention reaction time, or task-evoked responses), or a microstructural index of a structure (for example diffusion measures), separates MCI from a non-impaired comparator. The same measure under the simpler condition, or the corresponding volume, does not.

results.loaded_measure: Gait markers in single-task curved-path (oval) 10 m walking recorded by Kinect v2: average velocity, cadence, and mean/median step and stride velocity (also step time, stride time, double-support time and step width, mean and median).
results.simpler_or_static_measure: The same gait markers in single-task straight-path 10 m walking, same participants, same session protocol (three trials per path).
results.comparator: 30 healthy controls without cognitive impairment (IDAA comprehensive evaluation; MoCA 27.13 vs 22.76, MMSE 28.50 vs 25.60) against 25 MCI; age (p = 0.091) and sex (p = 0.216) not different.
results.dataset_family: Iran Dementia and Alzheimer's Association (IDAA) clients plus volunteers answering study notices; ethics Semnan University of Medical Sciences IR.SEMUMS.REC.1398.237 (2019-12-17); single site, not public (data on request).
results.method_family: Markerless depth-camera instrumented gait (Kinect v2, 25 joints, 50 macro/micro gait markers), straight vs curved single-task walking; per-marker t-test or Mann-Whitney with ANCOVA adjustment; ROC.
results.why: Identity: PDF title, authors (Seifallahi, Galvin, Ghoraani), journal and DOI 10.3233/ADR-230149 match the Paper 1082 block and the registry row (not a duplicate stub; peer-reviewed, not a preprint). Whole extract read (the extractor omits the reference list). The study runs the dissociation itself, in the same 55 participants, against a non-impaired comparator, and it holds marker by marker for the same markers under the two conditions, which is exactly the case the rules name (velocity in straight versus curved walking). Straight walking: velocity p = 0.780, cadence p = 0.247, step velocity mean p = 0.574 and median p = 0.139, stride velocity mean p = 0.177 and median p = 0.165. Curved walking: velocity p = 0.007, cadence p = 0.018, step and stride velocity mean and median all p < 0.001 (Table 2, p.6). The authors state the split themselves (p.11), and list velocity, cadence and the step/stride velocities among the markers significant only in curve walking (p.5). The dissociation is not confined to a subgroup. Straight walking separates the groups on other markers (20 of 50, AUC 0.78); under the brief that is a caveat, not a disqualifier, and for the markers claimed the straight-walking measure is null. Hence yes, with the caveats listed.
results.caveats: (1) The unloaded test is not blind to MCI: 20 of 50 straight-walking markers differ (step and stride length, step height, variability and regularity markers; e.g. stride length mean 74.02 vs 63.62 cm, p = 0.006) and straight walking gives AUC 0.78 against 0.83 for curve walking. Twelve markers even show the reverse pattern (significant only in straight walking, e.g. stride-time and stride-length regularity p < 0.001 straight, n.s. curved), so the finding is marker-specific, not 'curve walking detects what straight walking cannot' at test level. (2) About 100 per-marker group tests with no multiple-comparison correction; the straight-walking nulls are threshold nulls. (3) Adjustment is ambiguous: the Methods adjust for BMI, education and GDS by ANCOVA (p.3), the Table 2 note says values were adjusted for BMI only (p.6), and the printed means look unadjusted, so it is unclear which model produced each p. (4) The HC straight-walking velocity SD (27.92 cm/s) is implausible beside the HC step and stride velocity SDs (7.04, 7.22); the velocity null is nonetheless corroborated by the step and stride velocity nulls. (5) No formal condition-by-group test is printed for the claimed markers: the 'cost' analysis reports 13 markers whose SW-to-CW cost differs between groups (p.8) but does not list them or give statistics; the claim that the curve AUC is 'significantly higher' has no test statistic. (6) Groups differ on BMI, education and GDS (Table 1); MCI diagnosis by IDAA work-up without biomarkers. (7) Shared cohort: P-114 (Seifallahi et al. 2022, BSPC 71:103195) has the same first author, the same IDAA recruitment route (clients plus advertisement volunteers) and the same ethics committee (Semnan University of Medical Sciences), with 70 MCI / 80 HC recorded by Kinect v2; participant overlap cannot be determined from either text. P-114 was rated no in round 21, so this does not affect the supporter count, but the two should be treated as one dataset family. Notably P-114 found single-task straight-walking velocity DID separate MCI from HC (p < 0.001 per the round-21 reading), which cuts against generalising P-1082's straight-walking null. (8) No overlap in cohort, site or authors with P-651, P-665/P-687 or P-1163. Method-family note for the independence rule: this is loaded gait, as is the Guangzhou dual-task TUG (P-665/P-687); instrument (Kinect marker set vs stopwatch TUG) and load (path geometry vs concurrent dialling) differ, so whether they count as one method family is a classification call for the operator.

results.loaded_measure: Useful-Field-of-View reaction time (U-RT): button-press latency to a red target appearing at one of four peripheral locations 20 cm from centre (about 11 deg at 1 m) while gaze is held on a central fixation point; 80 trials.
results.simpler_or_static_measure: Central reaction time (C-RT): button-press latency to the identical red target presented at the centre of the screen; 20 trials, same trial timing, same participants.
results.comparator: 43 cognitively healthy controls (MoCA-J >= 26 and MMSE-J 28-30) against 31 MCI (MoCA-J <= 25 and MMSE-J 24-27); age 72.2 vs 73.4, p = 0.12.
results.dataset_family: Older adults residing in medical and nursing care facilities, Japan (Kyoto Tachibana University ethics 25-11; authors from Kyoto Tachibana, Morinomiya University of Medical Sciences Osaka and Naragakuen University); cross-sectional 2024-2025; data public on Mendeley Data (doi 10.17632/hnwrnk8mcw.1).
results.method_family: Computerised visual reaction-time paradigm (VRAS; central vs peripheral/UFOV detection) with head-mounted eye-tracking; t-tests, mixed-design ANOVA (task x group), ANCOVA with C-RT covariate, logistic regression and ROC.
results.why: Identity: title, authors (Tamaru, Inada, Ideguchi, Kagino, Katsuhara, Higashi), Scientific Reports 16:2330 and DOI 10.1038/s41598-025-32034-6 match the Paper 1163 block and the registry row (not a duplicate stub; peer-reviewed). Read in full to the references. The reworded statement names peripheral-attention reaction time as an example of a loaded condition, so the earlier family objection no longer applies. The study runs its own same-participant dissociation against a non-impaired comparator on the same marker (RT) under two conditions: central RT does not separate the groups (554.4 vs 568.5 ms, t = -1.22, p = 0.228, d = -0.29), UFOV RT does (580.3 vs 638.6 ms, t = -5.84, p < 0.001, d = -1.17). Unlike most candidates it also tests the dissociation formally: Task x Group interaction F(1,72) = 19.09, p < 0.001, partial eta squared 0.210, and the group effect on U-RT survives C-RT as covariate (F = 37.94, p < 0.001). No other central-task marker separates the groups (central omission p = 0.202, commission p = 0.577), so there is no unloaded-test separation to record. Not confined to a subgroup. Hence yes, with the caveats listed.
results.caveats: (1) Fixed order: the central task always came first (p.3), so practice, fatigue or time-on-task are confounded with condition; the Discussion says additional analyses rule out time-on-task (p.7), but Limitation 5 concedes the software gave only the overall mean U-RT, so 'we could not directly examine time-on-task effects' (p.7), an internal tension. (2) Unequal trial counts (20 central vs 80 UFOV); Fig. 1 caption says 'Each condition consisted of 20 trials', contradicting the Methods' 80 UFOV trials. (3) The peripheral targets sit about 11 deg off fixation, so retinal-eccentricity, sensory and oculomotor costs are not separated from attentional load; no visual-field testing beyond excluding visual impairment and corrective-glasses users; visual orienting frequency (gaze shifts) was higher in MCI at trend level (p = 0.052). (4) Groups were defined only by MoCA-J/MMSE-J cut-offs, which the authors call provisional (no consensus clinical diagnosis); participants were drawn from medical and nursing care facilities; single site. (5) The central-RT null is a threshold null (d = -0.29 with n = 74 is underpowered for a small effect), though the interaction test addresses this. (6) Sex split (21M/22F vs 18M/13F) not tested or adjusted; Table 1 prints an odd Cohen's d for age (-.0369). (7) The supplementary AUC comparisons with MoCA/MMSE are circular (those tests defined the groups), which the authors acknowledge; they are not used here. (8) The loaded condition is single-task peripheral detection under fixation, not a dual task; 'dual-task interference' is Discussion framing (p.7). This no longer matters under the reworded statement. (9) Independence: no overlap in cohort, site or authors with P-651 (Chongqing), P-665/P-687 (Guangzhou), P-1082 or P-114 (IDAA, Iran). The first author's earlier gaze-behaviour MCI paper (Tamaru et al. 2024, Sci Rep 14:19512, cited as ref 15 for the group criteria) is not in the corpus (no summaries.md match), so no corpus sample overlap was found. Method family (behavioural visual RT with eye-tracking) is distinct from diffusion MRI and from gait.

quotes.quote: For central reaction time (C-RT), the HC group had a mean of 554.4 ms (SD = 46.6), and the MCI group had a mean of 568.5 ms (SD = 52.6). This difference was not statistically significant (t = − 1.22, p = 0.228, Cohen's d = − 0.29). In contrast, for Useful-Field Reaction Time (U-RT), the HC group recorded a mean of 580.3 ms (SD = 44.9), while the MCI group had a significantly slower mean of 638.6 ms (SD = 38.4), indicating a significant group difference (t = − 5.84, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = − 1.17)

A mixed-design ANOVA with task condition (C-RT vs. U-RT) as the within-subject factor and group (HC vs. MCI) as the between-subject factor revealed a significant Task × Group interaction, F(1,72) = 19.09, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.210. This indicates that the group difference in response time was disproportionately larger for U-RT than for C-RT.
The covariate was significant, F(1,72) = 34.04, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.324, and the group effect remained highly significant after controlling for C-RT, F(1,72) = 37.94, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.348.

For central omission errors (C-OE), the median was 0.0 in both groups (interquartile range [IQR]: 0.0–0.0), showing no between-group variability. The difference was not statistically significant (U = 745.5, Z = 1.276, p = 0.202, r = 0.148).
For central commission errors (C-CE), no significant group difference was observed (U = 705.0, Z = 0.557, p = 0.577, r = 0.065).

In the UFOV task, the MCI group exhibited a slightly higher VOF (median = 3.0, IQR 2.0–3.0) compared to the HC group (median = 2.0, IQR 2.0–3.0). This difference approached but did not reach statistical significance (U = 833.0, p = 0.052, r = 0.230)

Inclusion criteria for the HC group were a score of ≥ 26 on the Japanese version of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA-J) and a score of 28–30 on the Japanese version of the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE-J). The MCI group included patients with MoCA-J scores ≤ 25 and MMSE-J scores 24–27
To minimize potential carry-over effects, the central visual field task was always presented first, followed by the UFOV task.

Condition 2 (UFOV task): A black fixation point of the same size remained at the center of the screen. While maintaining gaze on the fixation point, red circular targets identical to those in Condition 1 were presented in one of four peripheral locations—upper right (45°), lower right (135°), lower left (225°), or upper left (315°)—each 20 cm from center.
The C-RT task consisted of 20 trials and the UFOV task consisted of 80 trials.

Fifth, the stimulus presentation software provided only the overall mean RT for the 80 UFOV trials, which precluded analysis across smaller blocks of 20 trials. Consequently, we could not directly examine time-on-task effects.
Third, MCI classification was based solely on MoCA and MMSE scores. ... Therefore, our classification should be considered provisional

summary: Under the reworded VF-25 both papers answer yes. P-1082 (IDAA, Iran): the same gait markers (velocity, cadence, step and stride velocity) are null in straight walking and separate MCI from controls in curved walking, in the same 55 participants; caveats are that straight walking separates the groups on 20 other markers, uncorrected multiplicity, ambiguous covariate adjustment, and a shared recruitment route, first author and ethics committee with P-114 (a round-21 'no'). P-1163 (Japan): central RT null, peripheral UFOV RT separates, with a formal task-by-group interaction; caveats are fixed task order, unequal trial counts, eccentricity confound and screening-score-only group definitions. Neither shares a sample with P-651 or the Guangzhou P-665/P-687 sample. Whether P-1082's loaded gait and the Guangzhou dual-task TUG count as one method family is left to the operator.
